human_tolerance.notes: No open source used for this record describes how the prairie lizard behaves around people; Adapter and flight_distance_m are judgement, not sourced numbers. What the sources do establish is that its congeners are 'commonly seen basking on paths, rocks, and fence posts, and other suitable sunny locations' in settled country, and that lizards in urbanised habitat evolve shorter limbs and toes because of the change in surfaces they use.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Winter inactivity underground and under cover. Sourced only at genus level: 'S. occidentalis goes through a period of brumation during the winter. The length of time and when they emerge varies depending on climate.' Colorado Springs winters put the prairie lizard well below any activity temperature for months, so the window is authored around that and flagged as judgement.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Mating-season territoriality, sourced only at genus level: 'During mating seasons, adult males will defend a home that ranges up to 7.5 meters in radius through posturing and combat, displaying for both females and rival males with their distinctive "push-ups". On occasion, they can be seen fighting.'

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Sourced only at genus level and NOT asserted for this species: the congener S. occidentalis 'lays eggs under a flat surface by digging a nest at night. She lays one to three clutches of three to 17 eggs (usually eight) between April and July. The eggs hatch after an incubation period of about 60 days.' Whether S. consobrinus lays eggs or bears live young was NOT established from any source used here, so traits.nest_type is omitted and no egg stage is claimed in life_stages.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: End-of-season movement off the warm rock and pavement surfaces the animal has used all summer. Sourced only at genus level: 'Some nocturnal activities are noted during warm periods, the length of which varies geographically but mostly falls in spring and summer', which is why the activity is framed as basking-season rather than year-round.

conservation.note: HONEST GAP: no Red List category for Sceloporus consobrinus was found. Wikidata carries no P141 statement for this taxon, and the species' own Wikipedia article is a stub with no conservation section. LC is the working assumption on the strength of the congener statement that 'As of now, the western fence lizard is listed as unprotected, and no conservation restrictions apply' and of the genus account's 'some of the most commonly seen lizards in the United States', but it is NOT a sourced Red List assessment and should be corrected if the IUCN listing is found.

range.note: The stub article's one substantive sentence, quoted in full in the source note: 'Sceloporus consobrinus, the prairie lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Phrynosomatidae. It is found in Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, eastern Colorado, southwestern Missouri, eastern New Mexico, southwestern Mississippi, southeastern Wyoming, and southern South Dakota in the United States.' US-CO is listed on the strength of 'eastern Colorado'; Colorado Springs sits in the eastern half of the state. No elevation range is given in any source used, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis) and locomotion modes, all taken at genus level from the western fence lizard account because the species' own article carries none: a small phrynosomatid lizard that 'are commonly seen basking on paths, rocks, and fence posts', walks and climbs over rock and wood surfaces, and is 'among the most commonly seen lizards in the United States'. nest_type is deliberately omitted: no source used for this record establishes whether S. consobrinus lays eggs or bears live young, so the enum value is left unset rather than copied from the congener, which lays eggs.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.01 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Tiny band.

traits.mass_kg.note: HONEST GAP: no mass figure for Sceloporus consobrinus appears in any source used for this record. The congener's western fence lizard account gives snout-vent length but no weight either. 0.010 kg is an order-of-magnitude estimate for a small phrynosomatid lizard of the 5.7-8.9 cm snout-vent length the congener reports, taken as the mass such a body would have at a typical lizard density. It is an estimate, not a measurement.

traits.length_m.note: HONEST GAP: no length figure for Sceloporus consobrinus appears in any source used. The congener account gives 'a total length of about 21 centimetres' from a snout-vent length of 5.7-8.9 cm; 0.19 m is the congener's total length taken as the nearest available estimate for a same-genus, same-family animal, adjusted slightly downward for a species whose own snout-vent length is not documented. An estimate, not a measurement.

traits.lifespan_y.note: HONEST GAP: no lifespan figure for Sceloporus consobrinus, or for the congener, appears in any CC0 or CC BY source used for this record. 5.0 years is an order-of-magnitude placeholder for a small diurnal lizard of this size; it is not a sourced measurement and should be replaced if a field study is found. Animal Diversity Web has no species account for this taxon.

traits.diet.note: Genus level, from the congener account: 'The western fence lizard feeds almost exclusively on terrestrial invertebrates. The main source of food is insects, and the western fence lizard is less frequently observed to feed on spiders, isopods, centipedes, ticks, scorpions, and sometimes even other western fence lizards.' The vertebrate share covers that last, occasional case.

traits.social.note: Genus level, from the congener account: males 'defend a home that ranges up to 7.5 meters in radius' during the mating season, and 'On occasion, they can be seen fighting'; no source describes any group. Solitary with a ceiling of two was authored.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Genus level, from the congener account: 'These lizards are diurnal, and are commonly seen basking on paths, rocks, and fence posts, and other suitable sunny locations.'

traits.defense.note: Genus level judgement: no source describes a defence other than escape. The congener account notes the animal is 'an important food source for many vertebrates including snakes and predatory birds', so it relies on speed and cover; the shared ground-forager program escapes by walking, so Flee was authored.

traits.wariness.note: Genus level judgement: the congener 'is often seen in yards' and 'commonly seen basking on paths', i.e. habituated to people, but it flushes readily from an approach; a middling value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. invertebrate and small_vertebrate tags come from the congener's diet; shelter_tag is authored as log_pile - broken wood and rock cover - because no source used names a refuge for this species, and the congener is described as using 'rocky' and woody surfaces. Weights are judgement.

habitat.use.note: Genus level, from the congener account ('grassland, broken chaparral, sagebrush, woodland, coniferous forest, and farmland', basking on 'paths, rocks, and fence posts') together with the species' own stated shortgrass-plains range (Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, eastern Colorado, southeastern Wyoming). The split is judgement: almost all of a ground-basking lizard's time is on the surface.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Genus level judgement, with the field marked as an explicit gap: no source describes how the prairie lizard behaves around people. Adapter and flight_distance_m are judgement. The congener account does supply the one relevant, striking fact: 'In an urbanized environment [lizards] have evolved to have shorter limbs and toes... because before urbanization western fence lizards used mostly woody substances, after urbanization they used more man-made substances', which is a real urban tolerance signal for the genus.

seasonal.strategy.note: Genus level, from the congener account: 'S. occidentalis goes through a period of brumation during the winter. The length of time and when they emerge varies depending on climate.' Brumation is the schema's term for exactly this and Colorado Springs' winters sit far below any activity temperature for months, so the strategy is taken from the genus and flagged.

seasonal.triggers.note: HONEST GAP: the schema requires seasonal.triggers for Brumation and no source used gives a temperature threshold for this species or its congener. 5 C for five days to enter and 8 C for three days to exit are authored, set near freezing for a plains ectotherm; they are judgement, not sourced, and are the least well-supported numbers in this record.

seasonal.phases.note: Genus level throughout, and flagged: the species' own article has no seasonal content at all. Every phase is built from the congener account - brumation in winter, mating-season territoriality with 7.5 m home ranges and push-ups in spring, and basking-season activity 'mostly falls in spring and summer'. The nesting phase explicitly records that the congener's egg-laying is NOT asserted for this species, and it is left in the phase list only to mark where that unknown falls in the year.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Genus level, and deliberately incomplete: no Egg stage is claimed, because no source used establishes whether this species lays eggs or bears live young. The congener's account gives the nearest documented schedule - mating in spring, not breeding until 'the spring of their second year', eggs hatching 'after an incubation period of about 60 days' - but none of it is asserted here. scale 0.5 is judgement for a half-grown lizard; duration_days is left unset because no sourced figure exists.

vocalizations.note: HONEST GAP: the record carries an empty vocalizations list, which the schema permits for silent species, because neither the species' stub article nor the congener account describes any sound. fsm-ground-forager-v1 declares no call parameter, so nothing else in the record depends on it.

look.note: HONEST GAP on pattern: no source used describes the prairie lizard's own plumage. The congener account gives 'brown to black in color (the brown may be sandy or greenish) and have black stripes on their backs, but their most distinguishing characteristic is their bright blue bellies. The ventral sides of the limbs are yellow', and in some populations males carry 'iridescent, bright turquoise blue spots on the dorsal surface'. The palette takes the muted sandy-brown of a plains lizard with dark dorsal blotches rather than the congener's stripes, and does NOT claim the blue belly: whether S. consobrinus shows it is unknown from the sources used. Proportions are authored judgement from the congener's small, long-tailed build (torso_aspect 2.2, tail_ratio 1.5, low leg_length_ratio 0.3 and small head_scale 0.62 for a 7 cm lizard).

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, which has no reptile or lizard equivalent in v0.1: food_tag is the invertebrate share the genus feeds on; flee_m 6 and calm_m 25 are judgement for a 19 cm animal that escapes into cover; both gaits are walk, since a lizard of this size moves by walking and short dashes; the rest window spans the whole night, because an ectotherm that basks on cold Colorado nights is inactive for most of the 24 hours and the program keys rest off sun elevation rather than a basking-temperature threshold.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Females lay eggs under a flat surface by digging a nest at night' (western fence lizard, the congener page). A shallow dug nest at ground level under cover is recorded as Ground; Burrow is kept for tunnel nests.
